method: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases) 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement' (published 23 February 2025). Every claim is a paraphrase backed by anchors (scripts/anchor.py): verify.py --source re-finds each anchored span in a fresh copy of the source, checks the claim's numbers against it and rejects copying. LICENCE: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC12167611). The source's words are NOT reproduced here. Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from Box 4 (wound care, extracted as table 2) are paraphrased and anchored to its row lines.

claims.claim: **Suspect Buruli ulcer in a slowly progressive, classically painless nodule, plaque, swelling or ulcer on exposed skin (usually a limb)** in someone exposed to an endemic area; early lesions are often mistaken for insect bites. The incubation period averages about five months (1–9 months), so cases peak in winter.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Endemic areas are expanding:** the Mornington and Bellarine Peninsulas, Melbourne's inner north-west and Geelong, far-north Queensland near Cairns, and more recently Bateman's Bay in NSW. Victoria recorded 362 new cases in 2023.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Diagnose with IS2404 PCR on a swab taken around the undermined ulcer edge.** A negative PCR does not exclude it, especially in early lesions and children: biopsy non-ulcerated or PCR-negative suspicious lesions (centre of a nodule, margin of an ulcer) for PCR and to rule out other diagnoses such as malignancy.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Culture is less sensitive than PCR and can take up to 12 weeks.** Without PCR, a probable diagnosis rests on a compatible lesion, acid-fast bacilli on microscopy and endemic exposure.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **First line for most patients: eight weeks of oral combination therapy containing rifampicin** (high-quality evidence). Injectable regimens are no longer recommended; always use two drugs, never monotherapy.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Doses:** rifampicin 10 mg/kg a day (maximum 600 mg), plus one of clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg twice a day (maximum 500 mg 12-hourly), moxifloxacin 400 mg daily or ciprofloxacin 500 mg 12-hourly. Choose the partner drug on comorbidities, interactions and tolerability; clarithromycin is the preferred macrolide.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If rifampicin cannot be used, give clarithromycin plus a fluoroquinolone for eight weeks. In pregnancy, use rifampicin with clarithromycin.** Rifampicin has been PBS-listed for Buruli ulcer since November 2020.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Six weeks may suffice** for immunocompetent adults with a small ulcer (under 3 cm) or severe adverse effects, particularly alongside surgery. Avoid shortening when several risk factors for failure are present (weight over 90 kg, immunocompromise, rifampicin–clarithromycin, male sex); rifampicin with a fluoroquinolone may then be preferred.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **About 20% have drug toxicity** (higher over 65 years, in women and with renal impairment). Check FBE, liver and renal function at baseline; do a baseline ECG because clarithromycin and fluoroquinolones prolong QTc, repeating it at two weeks if at risk; renally adjust clarithromycin and ciprofloxacin.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Rifampicin interacts widely:** check every medicine, and advise alternative contraception for users of the oral pill or progestogen implant (a levonorgestrel IUD stays effective).
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Warn patients that ulcers usually get bigger on treatment and will not be healed when antibiotics stop.** Median healing in Australia is 4.5 months: about three months under 2 cm, four months at 2–4 cm, six months over 4 cm.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Aggressive surgery is no longer recommended,** but conservative debridement, narrow excision (usually after four weeks of antibiotics, allowing a shorter course for small lesions) or curettage still have a role, planned jointly with infectious diseases. Delay grafts or flaps until antibiotics are finished and the wound is healed or nearly so.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **About one in five patients develop a paradoxical reaction** (worsening induration, ulceration, pain, discharge or a new lesion after initial improvement). First exclude poor adherence; true failure in adherent patients is rare. Usually continue the same antibiotics at the same dose and duration.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **For severe, destructive reactions, give prednisolone 0.5–1.0 mg/kg daily, with a four-to-eight-week taper;** the antibiotic course can be lengthened to 12 weeks overall.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Children get oral rifampicin with clarithromycin at the adult dose and duration.** Alternatives used in paediatric centres: azithromycin 10 mg/kg (maximum 500 mg) daily, or ciprofloxacin 15 mg/kg (maximum 500 mg) twice daily. Liquid rifampicin is not PBS-subsidised for this indication.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Paradoxical reactions occur in 39% of children;** a severe reaction warrants daily prednisolone at 0.5 mg/kg, capped at 40 mg, weaned slowly over a month or more.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Clean the wound bed and keep it covered.** Removing necrotic and inflammatory tissue helps healing and helps prevent paradoxical reactions and secondary infection: use a pharmacy topical debrider (none is proven better), clinic debridement by an experienced clinician, or surgery, and wash with sterile water, saline or clean shower water. Cover open wounds with an absorbent, breathable dressing, changed every one to three days by exudate or sooner if it soaks through; keep tight clothes and shoes off fragile wounds until healing matures.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Keep the base moist but not macerated** (absorbent dressings for heavy exudate; honey is commonly used). For swelling, elevate the limb and use fitted compression if tolerated, and consider a diuretic for oedema from heart failure. Take a diet history, bring in a dietitian if nutrition is poor, and consider oral zinc and vitamin C.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Fix what slows healing:** in leg ulcers check pulses and venous drainage, and refer for imaging and specialist input if the blood supply looks poor; support quitting smoking and cutting down alcohol; make glucose control a priority and screen readily for diabetes; optimise HIV treatment and watch interactions. Keep an affected joint moving; immobilise only briefly after surgery, on surgical and physiotherapy advice.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Scars and other measures:** a regular emollient for everyone, silicone gel or sheeting where hypertrophic or keloid scarring is likely, and SPF 50+ sunscreen on the scar. Ulcers with much necrotic tissue are tetanus-prone, so offer a booster. Unusual or severe pain on treatment should prompt a search for deeper spread, secondary infection or a paradoxical reaction. Hyperbaric oxygen has no supporting evidence.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Advise mosquito-bite avoidance** (repellent, covering clothing, screens), gloves and long sleeves when gardening, prompt washing and covering of cuts, and minimal contact with native possums and their droppings.
claims.locator: Medical Journal of Australia (endorsed by the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases), 'Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement', published 23 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12167611/, retrieved 2026-09-23
